spine: The Minnesota investigation is neither ordinary policing nor totalitarianism; the vocabulary we reach for fails it, and the failure is the subject.
Democracies now lose liberal substance through law rather than against it, so "was it legal?" is the wrong test.
To govern is first to see: state capacity begins in legibility, and digital legibility has shifted from who you are to whom you appear beside.
No single eye watches; a modular, largely private ecosystem observes, and its political danger is interoperability, not any one camera.
Fusion converts observations into relationships; capacity grows combinatorially, and doctrine adapts behind the technology.
The right model is Fraenkel's dual state, not the police state: zones of thinned legal protection already exist, and immigration is the laboratory.
Some opacity between citizen and state is democratic infrastructure, not a consumer preference.
The checks matter until the day they do not; the moment to defend them is while they still do.
